items.name: cn
items.description: Class-name composer: merges conditional classes and resolves conflicting Tailwind utilities so a consumer's className always wins over a component's defaults.

items.name: chrome-control
items.description: The 32px chrome control: a square, softly-rounded button filled with --ui-bg-elevated and carrying no edge. Not a Button variant — every button type is either a fill with a matching edge or an edge on nothing, and this is the one shape that is a fill with no edge at all. It belongs to page chrome (a menu toggle, a back arrow, a calendar's month arrows) rather than to the action vocabulary. Exported as one recipe because it was independently reinvented four times before it had a name.

items.name: menu-surface
items.description: The menu surface: one panel recipe and one row recipe, shared by Menu and ContextMenu. Not two components that happen to look alike — Base UI's ContextMenu re-exports Menu's Item, Group, Separator and Submenu verbatim, so they are literally the same rows in the same popup, differing only in what opens them. A recipe rather than a component for the same reason chrome-control is: it styles, it does not wrap, so the behaviour layer keeps ownership of roles, roving focus, typeahead and dismissal.

items.name: compose-event-handlers
items.description: Composes a consumer event handler with component-owned behaviour. The consumer runs first and may prevent optional internal behaviour with preventDefault; non-cancellable safety invariants stay outside the helper.

items.name: use-controllable-state
items.description: The one implementation of the controlled/uncontrolled pattern (CONVENTIONS §4). Returns [value, setValue] with a referentially stable setter; a controlled component never updates its own state, and switching modes mid-life warns in development instead of silently picking a winner.

items.name: font-aspekta
items.description: Aspekta Variable — the design system's single typeface (SIL OFL 1.1, by Ivo Dolenc). Installs the @font-face CSS and the OFL license text; the ~30KB variable woff2 (weight 100-900) is binary and is fetched from the repo with the one-line curl documented at the top of aspekta.css, into the same directory. Keep OFL.txt with the font wherever it is deployed.

items.name: button
items.description: The primary action control. Five variants (primary, secondary, outline, ghost, danger), three sizes (44/32/24px), pill or rounded, plus icon-only and full-width forms. Icon-only buttons require an aria-label at the type level. isBusy is visual-only and keeps focus, unlike isDisabled.

items.name: header
items.description: The page's top bar: leading controls, an optional row of navigation items, trailing controls. A <header> so it is the banner landmark, but deliberately NOT a nav — the bar also holds a brand switcher and an avatar menu, and calling all of that navigation would make the landmark useless to skip to; the item row names itself. Header.MenuButton is the control the navigation COLLAPSES INTO: there is no rail, so below the breakpoint the Sidebar is removed rather than narrowed and this button is what remains of it, opening the same Sidebar inside a Sheet. An item is a real <a> when given an href and a <button> otherwise, because the design draws two carrying a chevron that open menus rather than navigate.

items.name: input
items.description: Single-line text field with its label, helper text and error message as one accessible unit. Three sizes (48/40/32px), leading and trailing slots. The label prop is required by the type system — a placeholder is not a label. errorText wires aria-invalid and aria-describedby together so the two cannot drift apart.

items.name: popover
items.description: A panel anchored to a trigger, for secondary content that should not take over the page. Compound: Trigger, Panel, Title, Description, Close. Positioning, focus restoration, dismissal and ARIA wiring come from Base UI (ADR 0012), wrapped so no third-party type reaches a public prop signature. Bare text inside the 32px-radius panel is inset one step; boxed children sit flush.

items.name: modal
items.description: A dialog that takes over the page: scrim behind, focus trapped inside, focus restored to the trigger on close. Compound: Trigger, Surface, Title, Description, Footer, Close. Always modal — a non-modal dialog with a scrim is a Popover. Dismissal by Escape and scrim-click is on by default and can be turned off for unsaved work. Built on the Base UI behaviour layer (ADR 0012), wrapped so no third-party type reaches a public prop signature.

items.name: multiselect
items.description: A filterable list of options where more than one can be chosen, with the selection shown as removable chips. Listbox/combobox ARIA, aria-multiselectable, active-descendant management, typeahead, filtering and dismissal all come from the Base UI behaviour layer (ADR 0012), wrapped so no third-party type reaches a public prop signature. The trigger reuses Input's control surface; chips are Badge components with real remove buttons.

items.name: select
items.description: Choose ONE value from a list. The trigger is Input's control surface, exactly as Multiselect's is — a field is a field, and three components inventing three variants of the same box is how a system stops looking like one. Listbox ARIA, typeahead, roving focus and dismissal come from the Base UI behaviour layer (ADR 0012), wrapped so no third-party type reaches a public prop signature.

items.name: avatar
items.description: A person or entity as a photo or their initials. Circle or rounded, three sizes. `name` is required in both forms — it is the image's alt text and the source of the initials. Initials are aria-hidden and the full name exposed separately, so a screen reader announces the person rather than spelling out letters.

items.name: badge
items.description: A short status or selection label. Four variants (selected, unselected, success, danger), two sizes, pill or rounded, with an optional trailing slot. Renders a span and takes no interaction props: anything actionable is a real button passed into iconEnd, keeping the accessible name at the call site.

items.name: banner
items.description: An inline message attached to the surface it belongs to — not a toast, not a dialog. Five intents (neutral, info, success, warning, danger), an optional leading glyph slot and an optional dismiss control whose accessible name is required at the type level. Announces only when isLive is set, so a banner rendered with the page does not talk over the user. Composes inside a Popover panel as a boxed child.

items.name: card
items.description: A titled surface that groups related controls. Renders a <section> with a real heading at a caller-chosen level, so a card is navigable structure rather than a styled div. Compound: Header (with an actions slot) and Footer, both carrying the unboxed inset while boxed children sit flush. The surface is deliberately identical to Popover's panel.

items.name: calendar
items.description: A month grid for picking one date, with month and year selects in its header. Ours rather than a library's (ADR 0012): the hard parts are the ARIA grid and the keyboard contract, and both are decisions this system has to own. One roving tab stop, arrows by day and week, Home/End across the week, PageUp/PageDown by month, and an arrow that walks off the edge carries the grid with it. The two header selects replace the grid in place at its own height, so the card never resizes; each is a listbox with its own roving stop and returns focus to its trigger. Month and weekday names come from Intl, so a consumer in another locale gets their own without this library shipping a translation table. Unavailable dates use aria-disabled and stay focusable — a date a screen-reader user cannot reach is one they cannot be told the reason for.

items.name: menu
items.description: A list of commands, opened from a trigger. The whole ARIA menu contract — role=menu and menuitem, roving focus, typeahead, Escape and outside-press dismissal, submenu timing and the aria-haspopup/aria-expanded wiring — comes from the Base UI behaviour layer (ADR 0012), wrapped so no third-party type reaches a public prop signature. Its panel and rows come from the shared menu surface, which ContextMenu draws from the same recipe, so the two cannot drift apart. Item.onSelect is named for the verb rather than for the pointer, because a menu row is chosen by keyboard as often as by mouse.

items.name: context-menu
items.description: The same menu, opened by a right-click on a region rather than by a button. Only three parts live here — Root, Trigger and Panel — because Base UI's ContextMenu re-exports Menu's Item, Group, Separator and Submenu verbatim; duplicating them would create two drawings of one surface. Requires the `menu` item for its rows. The keyboard path matters more here than anywhere else in the library: a surface that only opens on right-click is unreachable without a pointer, so Base UI opens it on Shift+F10 and the context-menu key as well.

items.name: date-picker
items.description: A date field that opens a Calendar. Two things this system already owns, composed: the field is Input's control surface — a field is a field — and the panel is the Calendar card itself rather than a second surface wrapped around one. Choosing a date closes the panel; clearing it deliberately does not, because the next thing that user wants is another date. Anchoring, dismissal and focus restoration come from Base UI (ADR 0012), wrapped so no third-party type reaches a public prop signature. The value is formatted with Intl by default and formatValue is the call-site escape hatch, so no date library ships with it.

items.name: card-sorting
items.description: A reorderable list of cards, with a grip on each row. Reordering works three ways and all three are first-class: a pointer drag, a keyboard lift-and-move (Space to lift, arrows to move, Escape to put it back), and a no-drag pointer path of click-to-lift then click-to-place, which is what WCAG 2.5.7 requires. Every path goes through one move and one polite live region that announces the row's name, its new position and the list's. Built without a drag library (ADR 0012) — the accessible half of this pattern is the half a drag library does not solve.

items.name: checkbox
items.description: A binary choice with its label as one control. Supports the mixed/indeterminate state for a parent whose children are partly selected. The whole row is the 24px target; the painted box stays 18px. Controlled or uncontrolled through the shared useControllableState hook.

items.name: switch
items.description: A control that takes effect immediately, unlike a Checkbox, which states an intention the surrounding form later submits. A native input with role=switch, so it is announced as on/off rather than checked. The whole row is the 24px target; the track stays 36x20. Controlled or uncontrolled through the shared useControllableState hook.

items.name: progress
items.description: A determinate progress bar with an optional label and percentage, in two track heights (20/8px). A div with role=progressbar and the three ARIA value attributes, because unlike a checkbox or a button a progress bar has no native behaviour to inherit. The value is clamped and the clamped value is what is announced.

items.name: sidebar
items.description: The primary navigation rail, built from ROWS rather than links: a row becomes an <a> when given an href and is otherwise a plain slot, because the design puts a search field in one and a progress bar in another. Sections carry the second level, optionally collapsible, at the same inset — hierarchy is type and colour, not indentation. The current page is announced through aria-current rather than fill alone. First consumer of the --ui-nav-* role family, so a themed portal re-skins its chrome by re-binding six roles. No roving tabindex and no menu roles — navigation is links, and the browser's own contract is worth more than arrow keys.

items.name: drawer
items.description: A panel that comes up from the bottom and is dismissed by dragging it down. Distinct from Sheet, and the distinction is the GESTURE rather than the geometry: a Sheet is anchored to a side edge and dismissed by scrim or Escape, while a Drawer carries a handle, follows the finger, and closes past a distance or velocity threshold. Base UI supplies the focus trap, scroll lock, Escape and focus restoration (ADR 0012); the drag is ours, with no drag library in the dependency list. The handle is a real button as well as a drag target, which is the single-pointer alternative WCAG 2.5.7 requires.

items.name: sheet
items.description: A panel that slides in from the left or right edge of the screen — the mobile counterpart to a Sidebar, which is what it usually holds. Third component on the Base UI behaviour layer, deliberately Modal's shape because the focus trap, scroll lock, Escape and focus restoration are the same problem; only the panel's position differs. Full height, 80% width capped at the rail's own, with the two INNER corners rounded so it reads as a drawer rather than a modal. It carries no chrome of its own: the design draws the back and close controls inside the navigation's own header band.

items.name: slider
items.description: A single-value slider in two track heights (20/8px), with an optional label and value. Pointer capture, keyboard stepping, Home/End, RTL and touch come from the Base UI behaviour layer (ADR 0012), wrapped so no third-party type reaches a public prop signature — the value is a number, never an array. The control is padded to a 24px target even when the painted track is 8px.

items.name: tabs
items.description: A segmented control that switches which panel is shown. Compound: List, Tab, Panel. Roving tabindex, arrow navigation, Home/End and the two-way tab-to-panel ARIA pairing come from the Base UI behaviour layer (ADR 0012), wrapped so no third-party type reaches a public prop signature. Activation is manual: arrows move focus, Enter or Space selects.

items.name: ui-craft
items.description: Agent skill: the craft rules for building interfaces with @bydiorama/ui — radii, elevation, motion, icons, hit areas, colour usage. Install so coding agents in your app apply the same polish standards as the design system itself. Adapted from jakubkrehel/skills (MIT), see CREDITS.md.
